Alpine lakes are among the most photographed landscapes in Europe, yet walkers on many of their shores spend more time on roads than beside the water. Around Lake Arnau, only about a third of the shoreline is publicly accessible; the rest belongs to private gardens, boathouses and clubs (Hürlimann, 2021, p. 14). The federal spatial planning act has asked cantons since 1979 to "keep lake shores and river banks free and to make public access and passage easier" (Art. 3), and successive cantonal laws have promised continuous lakeside paths. Four decades later, the paths remain fragmentary. This essay argues that the failure is not one of legal tools but of political will: the instruments to open the shoreline exist, but they require compensating a small number of well-organised owners for a diffuse public benefit, and that trade has repeatedly been lost at the ballot box.

# The legal promise

The constitutional basis for public access is weaker than its rhetoric suggests. Article 3 of the spatial planning act is a planning principle, not an enforceable right, and courts have consistently held that it must be weighed against the guarantee of property in Article 26 of the Federal Constitution (Moser & Gerber, 2019). In practice, this means that a canton may plan a lakeside path and expropriate the necessary strip of land, but it must pay full compensation and show that the path is proportionate — that no less intrusive route, such as an existing road, would serve the purpose.

Cantons have taken different routes. Thalberg's lake shore law of 1982 required municipalities to draw up shore protection plans and gave the canton the power to impose them where municipalities refused. Arnau, by contrast, relied for decades on voluntary agreements and on the gradual acquisition of plots as they came on the market. The difference is visible on the map: Lake Thalberg and Lake Brenz have long continuous public stretches, while the shores of Lake Arnau alternate between parks and walls (Keller, 2018, pp. 77–81).

# The politics of compensation

Why has expropriation been used so rarely? The answer lies in the distribution of costs and benefits. The benefit of a shoreline path is spread across hundreds of thousands of residents and visitors, each of whom gains a little. The cost falls on a few hundred owners, each of whom loses a lot — not only land, but privacy and, in their view, a part of the value they paid for. As Rasmussen's (1971) logic of collective action predicts, the concentrated interest organises more effectively than the diffuse one.

The 2016 cantonal vote in Arnau on the popular initiative "Lake shore path for all" illustrates the dynamic. The initiative would have obliged the canton to build a continuous path within twenty years and to fund it with at least six million francs per year. Owners' associations campaigned against it with the argument that the path would cost far more than projected and that paths through private gardens would be dangerous for children and unattractive for walkers. The initiative was rejected by 54 % of voters, with the strongest opposition in the lakeside municipalities themselves (Statistisches Amt, 2016).

Defenders of the status quo make a serious point that is often dismissed. Wyss (2020) writes:

> The demand for a continuous path treats the shoreline as a corridor, when it is in fact a mosaic of uses that have grown over centuries: boatyards, bathing places, gardens, reed beds. A path that cuts through all of them in the name of access may destroy precisely the variety that makes the shore worth walking along. The question is not whether the public should reach the water, but where, and at what cost to the shore itself. (p. 203)

Wyss is right that a path is not costless for the shore. Reed beds, which host many of the lakes' breeding birds, are protected precisely because they are fragile, and conservation authorities have opposed path sections that would pass through them.[^reeds] But this argument supports routing paths carefully, not abandoning them; and it is notable that it is rarely made about the private boathouses and lawns that already occupy most of the shoreline.

# What would work

If the obstacle is political, the remedies must change the politics. Three approaches have had some success elsewhere.

First, **pre-emption rights** allow the public to buy shore plots when they are sold, at the agreed market price, rather than expropriating unwilling owners. The canton of Morel introduced such a right for its lake shore in 2013; within ten years the canton acquired eleven plots and closed two of the largest gaps in its path (Dubois, 2023). Pre-emption is slower than expropriation, but it avoids the image of the state taking homes, which dominates every campaign against shore paths.

Second, **easements instead of ownership** reduce the cost. A right of way along the water's edge, limited to daylight hours and excluding bicycles, leaves the owner in possession of the land and much of its privacy. Courts in Thalberg have accepted such easements as proportionate, and compensation awarded for them has averaged under a fifth of the land value (Moser & Gerber, 2019, p. 341).

Third, **binding timelines with default plans** move the burden. In Thalberg, municipalities that did not adopt a shore plan within a fixed period had one imposed by the canton. This turned the question for local councils from "should we build a path?" into "where do we want it to run?", a question on which agreement is far easier.

# Conclusion

The fragmented shoreline of Lake Arnau is not the result of a missing law. It is the result of a political equilibrium in which a concentrated interest defends itself effectively against a diffuse one, and in which the legal instrument designed to break that equilibrium — expropriation with compensation — carries a political cost that few governments are willing to pay. The experience of Thalberg and Morel suggests that the equilibrium can shift when the public sector stops asking for the whole shoreline at once and instead uses slower, less confrontational tools: buying when owners sell, securing passage rather than land, and setting deadlines that change who must justify inaction. None of these produce a continuous path within a decade. All of them produce more shore than another failed initiative.
